name: Personal & Professional Development
description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
profile: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate student formation, namely, actively, consciously and ethically relating to oneself, others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhances critical thinking and independent learning. It also helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners. The course stimulates core academic skills, namely: Select and critically analyze academic sources Articulate research questions, thesis statements and arguments Improve communication skills through various forms of writing and speaking activities The course fosters personal, social and civic competencies, namely: Craft own academic and personal learning goals Critically reflect on own learning Develop effective collaborative learning approaches with peers, instructors and external partners Valuing community engagement, including the value of different knowledge types and perspectives
topics: value of different knowledge types; ethically orientate oneself; enhance critical thinking; first-year requirement; societal partners; personal

name: Business & Economy in the Age of AI
description2: This course examines how organizations are structured and evolve over time. It explores how organizational design relates to strategy, external environment, human behavior, culture, governance and performance. A particular emphasis is put on discussing the concept and enabling capabilities of organizational agility required to navigate a fast-paced world and tackle increased uncertainty.
profile: As we enter the “Age of AI,” this course explores AI’s business, managerial, economic, and societal implications. It is designed for UCR students with a strong interest in AI and requires no prior technical background. The course traces AI’s evolution from early research to generative AI, highlighting its capabilities and limits. Through real-world examples and business cases, students analyse AI’s impact on competitiveness, innovation, labour markets, economic growth, inequality, climate change and society. In this context, students critically examine AI governance and ethics, addressing issues such as bias, privacy, and fairness across business functions (e.g. Marketing, HR, Finance), while also exploring corporate governance and regulation more broadly.
topics: fairness across business functions (e; organizational agility required; tackle increased uncertainty; organizational design relates; enabling capabilities; external environment

name: Introduction to Economics
description2: Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.
profile: This course provides an introduction to the principles of economics. The first part of the course delves into microeconomics concepts, including supply and demand, game theory, theory of consumer behaviour, theory of the firm and market structure. The seco nd part of the course covers macroeconomics, beginning with an exploration of macroeconomics events and fundamental concepts such as aggregate output, unemployment and inflation rate. It then examines the dynamics of goods and financial markets in the short run.
topics: game theory; theory of consumer behaviour; theory of the firm; market structure; aggregate output; inflation rate

name: International Macroeconomics
description2: Study the economy as a whole through topics such as national income, economic growth, inflation, and unemployment. Understand how governments and central banks use fiscal and monetary policies to influence economic performance over time. The course also explores business cycles, international trade, and economic crises, preparing students to evaluate policy debates and global economic trends.
profile: This course explores the economy as a whole by examining its dynamics over the short, medium, and long run. Key indicators such as national income, economic growth, inflation, and unemployment are studied. The course analyses how fiscal and monetary polici es affect the economy. It also covers business cycles, economic crises, and international trade, providing the tools needed to interpret economic data, evaluate policy decisions, and understand global economic trends.
topics: national income; economic growth; unemployment are studied; business cycles; economic crises; international trade

name: Public Economics
description2: Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.
profile: This course examines the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy affects efficiency and equity. It explores the rationale for government intervention and key concepts such as market failure, public goods, externalities, taxation, p ublic spending, redistribution, and political economy. By combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, the course provides a framework for analysing the economic impact of public policies.
topics: market failure; public goods; p ublic spending; political economy; affect societal welfare; policies affect societal

name: Behavioral Economics
description2: This course integrates insights from psychology into economic theory to better understand how people make decisions. Learn how actual behavior deviates from the predictions of traditional economic models due to biases, heuristics, and framing. Through experiments, students will deepen their understanding of decision-making and its implications for economic theory and practice.
profile: This course integrates insights from psychology into economic theory to better understand how people make decisions. Learn how actual behavior deviates from the predictions of traditional economic models due to biases, heuristics, and framing. Through experiments, students will deepen their understanding of decision-making and its implications for economic theory and practice.
topics: decision-making; biases; heuristics; framing; behavioral experiments; economic choice

name: Marketing & Consumer Engagement
description2: This course unpacks what drives consumer engagement with brands and how marketers build customer trust responsibly. It introduces key marketing concepts, consumer psychology, AI/technology-driven marketing innovation, and brand and communication strategies. Students will explore real-life case studies, develop a strategic marketing plan and learn how marketers build sustainable brand strategies.
profile: Grounded in academic theory, real-world applications, and case studies, this course unpacks what drives consumers’ behaviour and engagement with brands, and how marketers can build customer trust responsibly. It introduces key concepts related to marketing strategy and consumer psychology and examines external forces influencing reinvention of the Marketing function, including digital and AI-driven marketing. Drawing on the work of Kotler, Aaker, Kapferer and other leading scholars, students will explore real-life case studies, develop marketing plans and learn how to create effective brand strategies for greater consumer engagement.
topics: ai-driven marketing; technology-driven marketing innovation; consumer engagement; customer trust responsibly; strategic marketing plan; sustainable brand strategies

name: Strategy & Digital Transformation
description2: The course explores how companies develop strategies and drive responsible digital transformation amid rapid technology change impacting the economy and society. Students develop a strategic plan, from vision to execution, and identify digital value opportunities. Using industry cases, they gain foresight into digital technologies and their impact on strategy, business models and social responsibilities.
profile: The course explores how companies develop strategies and drive responsible digital transformation amid rapid technology change impacting the economy and society. Students develop a strategic plan, from vision to execution, and identify digital value opportunities. Using industry cases, they gain foresight into digital technologies and their impact on strategy, business models and social responsibilities.
topics: digital transformation; transformation amid rapid; identify digital value; drive responsible digital; digital value opportunities; technology change impacting

name: International Business & Governance
description2: This course examines the institutional, political and cultural forces shaping global businesses. It first explores how international companies operate, then centers on key global challenges including cross-border governance, corporate responsibility, geopolitical strategies and global trade. It provides a comprehensive understanding of today’s complex international business environment.
profile: This course examines the institutional, political and cultural forces shaping global businesses. It first explores how international companies operate, then centers on key global challenges including cross-border governance, corporate responsibility, geopolitical strategies and global trade. It provides a comprehensive understanding of today’s complex international business environment.
topics: cross-border governance; corporate responsibility; geopolitical strategies; global trade; forces shaping global; international companies operate

name: Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations
description2: Through experiential learning, students turn their own bold ideas into new ventures. No prior business expertise is required as teams work on a startup project from ideation to final pitch while gaining business and entrepreneurial skills in areas such as design thinking, business model and customer validation. The class fosters creativity and collaboration to drive business and social innovation.
profile: In this course, you will develop a new venture idea from the ground up. No prior business experience is required – working in teams you will learn by doing, developing a startup concept from ideation through to the final pitch. Along the way, you will gain essential business and entrepreneurial skills, including design thinking, market validation and business planning. This course fosters creativity, business acumen and collaboration to drive business and social entrepreneurship.
topics: design thinking; market validation; business planning; class fosters creativity; prior business expertise; final pitch

name: Research Methods & Statistics
description2: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.
profile: Research Methods & Statistics is a general introduction in research methodology and statistics. The introduction to methodology includes the logics and design of research (e.g., operationalization, experimental design, sampling), and some specific techniques (e.g., laboratory research, surveys). The introduction to statistics includes descriptive and inferential statistics, covering measures of central tendency, spread, association, univariate and bivariate inferential statistics, and analysis of variance. This course includes an introduction to simple applications of multivariate statistics but most coverage of multivariate statistics and statistical modelling will be covered in the course HCBPSYC211 Statistics & Experimental Methods in Health & Behavioral Sciences. The first 9 course weeks (not including the semester break) of the course provide the theoretical background. This includes not only instruction and practice in basic research methodology and statistics, but also the planning stages of the group research projects that will dominate the latter portion of the semester. In this portion of the semester, students of each section attend two classes each week with their instructor. Project groups are formed, and these groups work together in applying newly learned concepts to their own research problem thru individually completed homework exercises, and through sharing and discussing their progress with the rest of the class. The final 6 course weeks are dedicated exclusively to group project work. This research project can fall within any academic discipline.
topics: research design; operationalization; sampling; experiments; surveys; descriptive and inferential statistics
methods: Research design; Operationalization; Experimental design; Survey research; Sampling; Descriptive statistics; Inferential statistics; ANOVA

name: AI Ethics
description2: Explores philosophical foundations and implications of AI. Examines the history of AI, ethical issues like interpretability, bias and alignment, debates about AI consciousness and implications for human nature.
profile: Developments in AI are transforming the nature of human interaction and raising fundamental questions concerning human flourishing and its alignment with technological progress. This course examines these issues from both philosophical and psychological pe rspectives, while exploring the deep connections between the two fields. In a module on the ethics of AI, we'll consider ramifications of the use of AI in the context of moral inquiry. Core topics include AI fairness and bias , privacy, responsibility and accountability . We will also approach the question concerning the moral status of AI systems , and some of the broader implications of AI, focusing on existential risks and broad political implications of the use of AI. In a module on psychology of AI, we will examine what it means to be human when AI systems increasingly mirror or simulate uniquely human capabilities. Research shows that people may both over-trust and resist AI in decision-making, which subsequently raises questions on responsibility and agency. In clinical and therapeutic contexts, AI challenges ideas of empathy, confidentiality, and the therapeutic alliance, while in organisational and social domains, algorithmic biases reflect and amplify existing stereotypes. Developmentally, AI companions and tutors shape how children learn and relate, prompting concerns about attachment and socialisation.
topics: ai fairness; like interpretability; alignment; implications; human nature; consciousness

name: Decision-making in AI
description2: Introduces planning techniques for AI systems in deterministic and non‑deterministic environments. Addresses uncertainty, partial observability, resource planning and optimizing behaviour under constraints.
profile: Introduces planning techniques for AI systems in deterministic and non‑deterministic environments. Addresses uncertainty, partial observability, resource planning and optimizing behaviour under constraints.
topics: non deterministic environments; partial observability; optimizing behaviour; addresses uncertainty; constraints; resource

name: Optimization Methods in AI
description2: Covers computational methods for search problems in complex and adversarial environments. Includes uninformed and informed search, local and global search, adversarial games and constraint satisfaction problems.
profile: Artificial Intelligence is concerned with building intelligent machines that can compute how to act effectively and safely in a wide variety of novel situations. Computer agents operate autonomously, perceive their environment, persist over a prolonged time period, adapt to change, and create and pursue goals. A rational agent is one that acts so as to achieve the best expected outcome. This course aims to provide the student with foundational abilities in: searching in complex and adversarial environment and optimizing by rational agents. Topics include uninformed and informed search in discrete and completely known environments, local and global search methods in unknown and continuous environments, games played in adversarial environments and constraint satisfaction problems. The second meeting of the class each week is entirely devoted to laboratory work where students tackle exercises and demonstrate their work. Projects are undertaken to provide experience of experimental investigations into areas such as graph search, constraint satisfaction, convex optimization, linear and non-linear programming. There are written Midterm and Final exams.
topics: informed search in discrete; completely known environments; global search methods in unknown; continuous environments; games played in adversarial environments; constraint satisfaction problems

name: Networks & Operating Systems
description2: Introduces computer networks and operating systems. Covers how the internet works and the role of an OS in resource management and application support.
profile: Computer networks are the foundations on which the modern commercial, entertainment, industrial, and social world is built. An operating system (OS) is system software that is the interface between computer hardware and applications. The first part of the semester is organized around layers of a computer network architecture. The main focus is on the Internet, its architecture and protocols are used for studying fundamental concepts. The second half of the semester starts by introducing the typical structure of an OS, by distinguishing between processes and threads, and by explaining how an OS schedules work. Then consideration is given to the issues of concurrency, memory management, and file systems. By the end of the course a student will have obtained a reasonable familiarity with how the Internet works and how the Internet can be monitored and controlled, moreover, a sound understanding of the pivotal role an OS plays in the managing of resources and the running of applications.
topics: operating systems; internet works; networks; support; resource management; computer

name: Database Management Systems
description2: Introduces relational database management systems and SQL. Covers relational database theory, authorization, normalization and query processing.
profile: Introduces relational database management systems and SQL. Covers relational database theory, authorization, normalization and query processing.
topics: relational database theory; query processing; database management systems; relational database management; covers relational database; normalization

name: Algorithms & Data Structures
description2: Teaches design and analysis of algorithms and data structures, emphasizing performance analysis and focusing on prominent algorithms and data structures.
profile: This course aims to provide the student with knowledge, skills and critical thinking ability in algorithm design and analysis. Inappropriate choice of algorithm and associated data structure can seriously impact on the performance of an application. The st udy of algorithm design and analysis provides techniques which help minimize the execution time of an algorithm. An emphasis is on the experimental performance analysis of algorithms. The second meeting of the class each week is entirely devoted to laboratory work where students tackle exercises and demonstrate their work. Larger algorithm projects are also undertaken. There is a written midterm exam and a written final exam. By the end of the course a student will have obtained an understanding of how algorithms have helped shape the modern world.
topics: data structures; emphasizing performance analysis; algorithms; prominent; teaches design

name: Introduction to Data Science
description2: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.
profile: Data science provides tools for extracting meaningful information from data. In this course, you develop foundational abilities in data visualization as well as data cleaning and manipulation. Next to traditional data coming in the form of tables, we explore non-traditional data types such as spatial data and text data. The course includes much hands -on work with example data sets coming from sciences, social sciences, and arts and humanities. At the end of the course, you carry out your own research project in which you apply your data analysis and visualization skills to answer a research question.
topics: spatial data; text data; data visualization; datasets; cleaning; manipulation

name: Machine Learning
description2: Covers core machine learning techniques from linear regression to advanced tree‑based methods. Discusses strengths and weaknesses and applies methods to real data from fields like medicine, physics and economics.
profile: Machine learning concerns an ever -expanding set of tools for understanding data and making predictions. This course introduces the fundamentals of machine learning. It presents several of the most important modelling and prediction techniques, along with several relevant applications. Topics include linear regression, classification, resampling methods, shrinkage approaches, tree - based methods, support vector machines, clustering, and more. Real-world examples are used to illustrate the methods, their strengths, and their limitations.
topics: linear regression; resampling methods; shrinkage approaches; tree - based methods; support vector machines; advanced tree based

name: Neural Networks & Deep Learning
description2: Explores theory and practice of neural networks. Students build basic networks and progress to complex networks for computer vision, and discuss recent developments in large language and image generation models.
profile: Neural networks have enabled major advances in areas such as computer vision, large language models, and generative AI. This course focuses on the underlying theory as well as practical implementations in the Python programming language using packages such as TensorFlow . No familiarity with Python is assumed, but a willingness to learn and write code in Python is essential. In the first part of the course, w e start by building and training our own basic neural networks from scratch. We also use TensorFlow to create bigger networks and apply them to tabular data. In the second part of the course, we move on to more complex neural networks for applications such as computer vision and text classification . We also discuss recent developments in large language models (such as ChatGPT) . Finally, if time per mits, we have a brief look at image generation models (such as DALL-E).
topics: computer vision; large language models; generative ai; text classification; discuss recent developments; neural networks

name: Introduction to Programming
description2: Introduces programming and computer science. Covers structured programming, data constructs, testing, debugging and object‑oriented programming with Python, and develops computational problem‑solving skills.
profile: This is the gateway course of Computer Science and AI studies; an introductory course in problem solving and computer programming in Python. The course begins by introducing traditional structured programming and data constructs (i.e. branching, loops, functions; tuples and lists). Then consideration is given to testing and debugging and finally the object- oriented programming constructs. During the entire semester, elements of discrete mathematics (e.g., logic, sets, enumeration) as well as certain computational problem solving techniques are also incorporated into the course material. There are classes twice a week. The first half of each class is a lecture where we learn new material, while the second half is devoted to laboratory work where students tackle programming exercises and demonstrate their work. Homework comprises weekly programming exercises and online quizzes. Two larger programming projects are undertaken. There is a written Midterm exam and a written Final exam. By the end of the course a student will have obtained a reasonable familiarity with the Python programming language as well as important concepts of discrete mathematics and computational problem solving techniques.
topics: object oriented programming; computational problem solving; covers structured programming; data constructs; python; debugging

name: Mathematical Methods
description2: Introduces linear algebra (vectors, matrices, eigenvalues) and calculus (limits, differentiation, integration) to construct and solve equations. Provides problem‑solving skills applicable across disciplines.
profile: Mathematics is the language used to grasp understanding of, to explore, and to gain insight in any of the sciences: physics, chemistry, biology, as well as engineering. None of these can be well understood or appreciated without sufficient skills in mathematics. The aim of this introductory course in the mathematics track is to learn basic widely-used mathematical techniques, such as differentiation, various techniques for integration, complex numbers and differential equations. These techniques are put into context in projects related to real situations in the fields of physics, chemistry, biology, economics, sociology, etc. In this course students will continue to construct knowledge on their mathematical bases already founded. Students will solve many problems as homework assignments. Furthermore, two exams will assess the students for their level of understanding and their ability to solve relevant mathematical problems. A lot of class time will be used to solve and discuss textbook problems. 3
topics: various techniques for integration; complex numbers; differential equations; solve equations; problem solving; linear algebra

name: Probability & Statistics
description2: Provides a foundation in mathematical statistics. Covers probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation; uses computer algebra software to develop theoretical understanding and practical skills.
profile: Provides a foundation in mathematical statistics. Covers probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation; uses computer algebra software to develop theoretical understanding and practical skills.
topics: probability theory; continuous distributions; parameter estimation; computer algebra software; statistics; covers probability

name: R3: Recycling, Recovery, Remediation
description2: Examines strategies and technologies towards a circular economy. Explores resource security and stewardship, develops lab skills and inorganic chemistry knowledge, and connects to themes at the Delta Climate Center.
profile: Examines strategies and technologies towards a circular economy. Explores resource security and stewardship, develops lab skills and inorganic chemistry knowledge, and connects to themes at the Delta Climate Center.
topics: delta climate center; inorganic chemistry; circular economy; resource security; stewardship; connects

name: Governance of Sustainability
description2: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
profile: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions. The first part of this course introduces you to the basic conceptual tools for understanding governance and to the major fault line in tackling sustainability problems as identified by Charles Mann in “The Wizard and the Prophet”. Wizards are techno-optimists who believe humanity’s creativity can tackle every challenge, whilst Prophets argue that humans should take a holistic and systemic approach that calls for a drastic reduction of exploiting the earth resources to respect planetary boundaries. In the second part of the course, we use Problem Based Learning to examine governance solutions to concrete sustainability challenges regarding food, freshwater, energy, and climate change.
topics: how are sustainability policies on the local; international level made; enforced? which actors represent which interests; how does public opinion shape politics? what; at the end of the day; determines effective policy

name: Sustainable Farming & Innovation
description2: Discusses environmental impacts of agriculture and explores sustainable agriculture approaches such as agroecology, organic farming, conservation agriculture, precision agriculture, sustainable livestock farming, agroforestry, permaculture, crop rotation, integrated pest management and sustainable supply chains.
profile: The production of food is a contentious topic in our modern society. Current farming methods are major contributors to environmental harm worldwide. However, the human population is expected to continue to grow to 10 billion before peaking, with the greatest growth forecast in developing countries. Sustainable farming is the approach where both food needs and environmental impact are balanced. As current farming practices are generally more concerned about output than impact, change is necessary to ensure a sustainable future, while still ensuring the human population can be fed adequately. In this course we will learn about and discuss different aspects of farming that contribute to future plans and directions of sustainable farming on a global scale. Current practices and environmental impacts will be presented, to understand where we are starting from. Current alternatives will be critically assessed, to understand how we might progress. Innovations and modern approaches will be researched, to understand where we might end up. The purpose of this course is not to convince you of what the right way forward is, but to present information objectively, so that you can make up your own mind and help build a more sustainable future.
topics: sustainable livestock farming; integrated pest management; sustainable supply chains; organic farming; crop rotation; precision agriculture

name: Earth Observation
description2: Provides hands‑on experience with GIS and data integration using geospatial data from satellites and drones. Uncovers how human actions impact ecosystems and climate and promotes sustainable practices through research projects.
profile: This course serves as a 200-level elective within the Environmental Science unit of the Environment and Sustainability Cluster. Geospatial data and images from satellites or drones are widely used to explore and model changes in the Earth’s system at various scales. This course focused on hands-on experience with GIS and data integration techniques. We will explore, visualize, and analyze how human actions can impact global ecosystems and climate, and how tools like ArcGIS pro can promote sustainable practices like soil/water governance and coastal protection planning by combining data from different fields. This course includes practical exercises, a final exam and a case study based on earth science-focused research question.
discipline: Remote Sensing; Earth Science; Environmental Science
topics: promotes sustainable; human actions; geospatial data; uncovers; satellites; drones

name: Environmental Biogeochemistry
description2: Investigates natural waters and their interactions with rocks, soils and minerals. Examines biogeochemical processes and cycles, including weathering, mineral formation, absorption, water treatment and resource recovery; utilises geochemical modelling and a case study.
profile: This course focusses on the biogeochemical processes on the earths surface. Most are related to soil-mineral-rock water interactions under near Earth -surface conditions. Biological and chemical controls on mineral formation processes will be studied in further detail as well as adsorption and leaching of nutrients or metals. Furthermore, (waste) -water treatment and engineered processes to recover valuable resources from waste, as well as some anthropogenic resource cycles are topics of this course. The theoretical and practical knowledge taught in SCIEART201/202 will be supplemented by using advanced geochemical modeling tools such as G eochemist Workbench. This course is very suitable for students in chemistry, geology and environmental science. The course may include some simple lab experiments, furthermore (in-class) exercises, one quiz and a case study.
topics: g eochemist workbench; valuable resources from waste; utilises geochemical modelling; investigates natural waters; mineral formation; water treatment

name: Sustainability Essentials I
description2: Provides key concepts in physics, chemistry, materials science, mathematics and modelling necessary for sustainability. Uses a case study to connect concepts to real‑world sustainability challenges and prepares students for 200‑level sustainability courses.
profile: ENSGATE101 - Sustainability Essentials serves as the Gateway course to all 200 level courses in the Environment and Sustainability Cluster. For that purpose we will discuss the tools and knowledge you need to follow and enjoy all 200 level course in the cluster. We will use the model of planetary boundaries to discuss the concepts of sustainability with an anthropogenic focus. The planetary boundaries concept was presented in 2009 and provides a novel synthesis of the most pertinent global environmental challenges by analysing the risk of crossing critical thresholds in the behaviour of the Earth system’s processes. These boundaries act as a framework to define a "safe operating space for humanity," highlighting the limits within which human development can occur without causing catastrophic harm to the planet. 3
topics: modelling necessary; materials science; prepares; sustainability; physics; mathematics

name: Sustainability Essentials II
description2: Builds on Sustainability Essentials I. Applies tools and knowledge to a real‑world sustainability case study and allows students to delve deeper into aspects connected to their field of interest.
profile: ENSGATE201 - Sustainability Essentials II serves as the Gateway course to several 300 level courses in the Environment and Sustainability Cluster. For that purpose we will discuss the tools and knowledge you need to follow and enjoy these course in the cluster. We will focus on three main topics (Waves, Chemistry and Material science) and on how they relate to Sustainability. You will have the opportunity to explore the topics in individual reflective journals as well as a project at the end of the course. In the project, you will use what you learned to analyse and discuss green washing. 3
topics: sustainability essentials; delve deeper; aspects connected; builds; allows; sustainability case

name: Climate Change
description2: Focuses on drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change on sea level, ocean acidification, ecology and society. Discusses adaptation and mitigation solutions, including renewable energy systems, carbon storage and climate‑adaptive planning, and examines climate governance and justice.
profile: Climate change is the defining challenge of our time. It has large impacts on both the living and non-living Earth systems, as well as drives a number of profound societal transformations. This course is roughly divided in 3 parts. First, we will first focus on the drivers of anthropogenic climate change and its impacts on the natural world. Topics discussed include (but are not limited to) the properties of greenhouse gases, sea level rise, ocean acidification, climate feedback loops and effects on various biome types. Secondly, we will discuss impacts on various aspects of society. Topics discussed include (but are not limited to) food production, transportation, construction, health, and migration patterns. We will discuss climate governance and -justice. We will also look at the history of the climate change debate and identify strategies that have been deployed by interest groups to sow doubt and misinformation. Lastly, we will look into solutions for both adaptation and mitigation, such as renewable energy systems, carbon dioxide storage and climate-adaptive spatial planning. The course will include a number of guest lectures and excursions. After taking the course, you will be able to explain the fundamentals of climate change science. You will also be able to navigate a vast flow of information on climate change, and identify main and reliable sources; you will have insight in main climate change issues and have an overview of the pathways to mitigation and adaptation.
topics: renewable energy systems; carbon dioxide storage; climate-adaptive spatial planning; anthropogenic climate change; ocean acidification; carbon storage

name: Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy
description2: Teaches evaluation of environmental impacts of products, processes and services throughout their lifecycle. Emphasises strategic planning for a circular economy through hands‑on learning.
profile: To prepare our society for a circular and sustainable future, we need to evaluate the environmental impact of products, processes, or services throughout their entire lifecycle, from raw material extraction to final disposal, or ideally re-usage as new raw materials. To do this, we have to understand the environmental, social and health consequences of products and processes and develop a strategic planning for future activi- ties. ENSSUST112 - Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economywill be heavily focussed on “learning by doing”, rather than by just studying books. Therefore most of this course will consist of analysing different products, processes and services and include guest lectures by experts working in the field of sustainability and circularity. 3
discipline: Industrial Ecology; Circular Economy; Sustainability Science
topics: circular economy; teaches evaluation; emphasises strategic; services; lifecycle; products

name: Calling Bullshit
description2: Develops skills to recognise and handle misinformation. Discusses cognitive biases and detection methods, distinguishes real from fake experts, and includes case studies and a video project tackling a misinformation topic.
profile: The world is rife with misinformation. To function properly in any field, it is important that you are able to recognize it adequately handle it. In this course, you will develop your “bullshit-detector”. The course is structured around the following four questions: What is bullshit? The word “bullshit” is subject to a lot of philosophical essays, of which you will read some. It is important to get a clear view of what we mean by it, and what distinguishes it from lying, fake news, mis/disinformation, nonsense or baloney, false beliefs, or the slightly different “horseshit”. We will discuss this extensively in the first sessions. We will then proceed with a historical overview of misinformation and the role it played in politics and society as a whole. It is -kind of- reassuring that bullshit is nothing new: Fake news and smear campaigns can be traced back to Sumerian clay tablets and were prominent in Roman society (ask Mark Anthony!). Understanding the historical context enables us to recognize patterns. What makes us vulnerable to bullshit? We will discuss common biases in human thinking and social pressures that make us vulnerable to bullshit and other types of misinformation. We are all human, so everybody can fall victim to false beliefs. Understanding our own way of thinking and the way our social environment influences us, helps us to process information more reliably and sharpens our critical thinking skills. How can you recognize bullshit? You will learn how to detect and distinguish several types of bullshit using a taxonomy of bullshit.
topics: misinformation; cognitive biases; fake news; pseudoscience; scientific credibility; critical thinking

name: Renewable System Design
description2: Teaches assessment of energy usage patterns and strategies for reducing consumption or transitioning to cleaner energy. Explores solar, wind and bioenergy solutions and includes technical and economic analysis; students deliver a report and presentation to a partner company.

name: Research in a Sustainable Delta
description2: In this project course you will work in small teams of two or three students on a research problem relevant for sustainability in the broadest sense. We are looking for collaborations with local companies and other institutions. The research questions are supplied by a regional institution or company that is active in areas related to sustainability in the broadest sense. In this way it is guaranteed that the research projects are indeed relevant for the Zeeland delta. Furthermore, students will have access to expertise and/or facilities of the external partner, which will broaden their perspective. Usually, there will be one person affiliated with the external partner organization involved with a project team as external advisor

name: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
description2: Offers a legal, historical and philosophical approach to human rights. Studies classical and modern philosophers, traces the rise of human rights, examines the US Bill of Rights and the French Declaration, and discusses human rights treaties.
profile: This course offers a broad approach to human rights: the legal, the historical and the theoretical/philosophical. In the first part of the course, human rights will mainly be studied in a legal way, adopting a legal perspective. Students will be introduced to the catalogue of human rights as positive law. Human rights treaties, the monitoring mechanisms and case law on human rights will be explored. This knowledge will be tested in a mid-term exam (multiple choice). In the second part, students will delve into a more historical and philosophical understanding of human rights. We will investigate the rise of the language of human rights in the 17th and 18th century, its culmination in the US Bill of Rights (1791) and the Déclaration des Droits de l’Homme et du Citoyen (1789). We will explore the further developments of the language in the 20th century in particular, which brought a great extension of the number and application of human rights. Students will read landmark cases that touch upon contentious, and often politicised disputes between liberty and equality. Some emphasis in this course will be given to natural law and its connection to human rights. We will delve into the classical and medieval scholarship on natural law, starting with Plato’s and Aquinas’ views on right and wrong. This will be compared to the modern views on the same going back to Hobbes and Locke, the latter considered to be the founding father of the rights paradigm. Human rights in today’s traditional societies will be investigated through selected case studies.
topics: human rights; french declaration; rights treaties; modern philosophers; traces; classical

name: Ethics
description2: Explores theories of moral reasoning—virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism—and discusses moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. Applies theories to practical issues such as animal rights, privacy, future generations, war, punishment, disability and equality.
profile: Our actions and decisions are structured by the ways we think about values, about what the good is. This course explores theories of moral reasoning, building upon historical and contemporary sources. In the first part of the course, we will examine the main theories in ethics – virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism – as well as questions pertaining to moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility, feminist contributions to ethical theory, the challenge of nihilism, and the relation of happiness and pleasure to ethics. The second part of the course largely focuses on practical ethics, touching upon topics such as equality, animal rights, poverty and wealth, future generations, climate change, historical injustice. We will examine our attitudes to these contentious and challenging issues, the way the topics relate to each other, and the manner in which questions in practical ethics highlight and bring into focus broader concerns pertaining to moral, political, and legal theory. Students taking the course will acquire in-depth knowledge of ethical theories, to be assessed through a mid-term exam. They will also work on developing research skills in papers and presentations, analyzing and assessing arguments from ethical theory and practical ethics while articulating an independent, informed perspective. Towards that end, throughout the term students will compose two reflection papers concerning topics in ethics, and in the second part of the term students will develop a research project comprising a final argumentative essay and a presentation.
topics: animal rights; future generations; climate change; historical injustice; moral reasoning virtue; reasoning virtue ethics

name: Foundations of Comparative Politics
description2: Provides analytical tools to compare political systems and democracies. Examines phenomena like democratic backsliding, decline of political parties, rise of populism, media changes, non‑majoritarian institutions and globalization’s impact on domestic politics.
profile: All over the world people seem increasingly dissatisfied with the way their political system works, whether its citizens in Bangladesh who ousted the Hasina government, or voters in consolidated democracies like Sweden who are increasingly voting for parties at the left and right extremes of the political spectrum. How can we understand and explain these developments? Foundations of comparative politics provides you with the key analytical tools to analyze and compare political systems and the development and functioning of democracies in particular. This is done using the research tools of ‘mainstream’ political science: theory driven qualitative and quantitative empirical research that seeks to describe and/or explain political phenomena. The course provides an overview and analysis of the core structures and institutions of political systems by examining the position of the state and studying its internal structures and functioning and its interaction with society. We examine these issues using the conceptual toolbox of comparative politics. We familiarize ourselves with the basic institutions that make up political institutions, and the way democracies and authoritarian regimes develop and can break down. We examine the functioning of consolidated democracies and the challenges they face from developments such as the decline of political parties, mediatization, the rising importance of non- majoritarian institutions such as courts and impact of globalization and internationalization on the capacity of domestic governments to act.
topics: decline of political parties; impact of globalization; non majoritarian institutions; phenomena like democratic; like democratic backsliding; compare political systems

name: European Union Politics
description2: Introduces EU politics. Outlines actors, institutions and decision‑making rules; examines responses to crises; and employs various approaches to study EU politics and policy‑making.
profile: This course introduces you to the European Union, a body politic that has been characterized as diverse as Unidentified Political Object, an unimperial empire as well as a superstate. Whatever its nickname , the EU is as political as any other body invested with public authority. For political scientists this means that it is vital to understand its functioning and to see where power is exercised and how various state and non-state interests try to get their preferences turned into policies. In the first part of the course we outline key actors, institutions and decision -making rules and show how political scientists have employed various ways to study EU politics and policy- making. Students will engage in Navigating the EU exercises that show them EU politics in the making and the sources to be used for that. In the second part of the course we will more directly examine the clash of interests through a group based research project where you study a legislative dossier and the interaction between interest groups and Members of the European Parliament, using the E Us transparency register . A key focal point in this analysis concerns the relative power of business interests vis a vis other interests in EU - decisionmaking and assessing what this implies for the legitimacy and effectiveness of EU - policies.
topics: decision making rules; outlines actors; politics; policy making; employs; responses

name: Introduction to Sociology
description2: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.
profile: Sociology provides a diverse and intricate toolkit composed of concepts, methods, and theories, which aids in comprehending and dissecting the functioning of societies on a local scale and the complex interconnections triggering global phenomena. Unlike disciplines like economics or political science, the subject of sociological inquiry is less clearly de fined. It encompasses all facets of human engagement within society, spanning from everyday interactions to the most longstanding social institutions. As a result, the wealth of knowledge within sociology can feel daunting, leaving one uncertain about where to begin. The course follows the recommendations 3 of the Sociological Literacy Framework 1, which is composed of the essential concepts and competencies in the discipline, as portrayed in the following table: Furthermore, this course overviews some of the most impactful sociological theories, including those by Marx, Weber, Durkheim, and Du Bois. It recognizes the social and historical backdrop that shaped these “classical” sociological ideas and concepts, notably influenced by imperialism and colonialism. This historical context notably sidelined the voices of BIPOC (Black, Indigenous, and People of Color) and women. Consequently, fundamental concepts like race and gender received inadequate theoretical attention within “classical” sociology. To bridge this gap, the course will prioritize students ’ interests and intellectual needs.
topics: those by marx; du bois; authors like marx; socio historical context; encourages exploration; social problems related

name: Qualitative Research Methodology
description2: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
profile: Similar to their quantitative counterparts, qualitative researchers ask basic, but demanding, questions before they start making any enquires, e.g. What is truth? What is reality? What is knowledge? Why do we want to conduct research? What do we want to get out of it? In contrast to quantitative studies, however, qualitative researchers are less interested in numbers, trends and generalisations. Instead, they are keen to explore the messiness of social processes: what motivates people to take actions, how people make sense of their world, and how politics, history and cultures influence people’s thinking and actions. In this course, we will critically examine the four key stages of conducting qualitative research: (1) research design and preparation; (2) data collection and management; (3) data analysis and interpretation, and (4) research dissemination. Throughout the course, students are expected to take an active role – to form a research group and choose a research topic, to interrogate qualitative research theories and their own research experiences, and to critically reflect the research processes and students’ own positionality, biases and assumptions. At the end of the course, students will share their research findings and experiences with one another.
topics: qualitative research methodology; conducting small team; interpreting meaning; power dynamics; reflecting; covers designing

name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
description2: Examines contemporary sociological debates about civil society through critical tradition, neo‑functionalism and decolonial critiques. Includes research group projects with NGOs or civil society organizations that translate conceptual insights into empirical analysis.
profile: The course ‘GOSSOCI311 New Issues in Contemporary Sociology’ builds upon the topics covered in ‘GOSSOCI101 Introduction to Sociology’ and ‘GOSSOCI202 Modern Sociology’. Its primary goal is to familiarise students with significant debates in sociological theory from a global perspective. This edition of the course focuses specifically on the idea of civil society, examining topics such as solidarity, social capital, social trust, the public and civil sphere, and civil repair in modern societies. The first part of the course explores a critical approach to civil society, starting with Gramsci’s ideas, followed by Habermas’s ideas on the public sphere and Fraser’s critique. It will examine cases in the Global South, and we will watch and discuss a movie about the power of grassroots civil society. The second part focuses on Alexander’s work on the Civil Sphere, cases of civil repair in Latin America, and performances of solidarity with migrants along Europe's southern border. The final part will explore the decolonial critique of the classical approaches to civil society and the civil sphere. Alongside the theoretical component, the course also includes an empirical aspect. Students will select an NGO, voluntary organisation, or other Civil Society Organisation (CSO) to explore the concepts covered in the course and the challenges associated with the work undertaken by these organisations. Using a Community Engaged Learning (CEL) approach, students will observe and study an organisation throughout the semester to gain an understanding of its culture, impact, and challenges.
topics: in ‘gossoci101 introduction to sociology’; ‘gossoci202 modern sociology’; social capital; social trust; civil sphere; civil repair in modern societies

name: Statistics & Experimental Methods
description2: The course is necessary for students who want to pursue master programs in psychology and adjacent disciplines, as well as research masters in the medical domain. It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers in other domains. In addition to technical training, the course emphasizes clear academic communication. It will equip you with the skills necessary to apply advanced statistical techniques to real-world research problems. With a focus on practical application through case studies and data analysis projects, You will be able to choose the appropriate statistical model for various research scenarios and address common challenges in data interpretation.
profile: The course is necessary for students who want to pursue master programs in psychology and adjacent disciplines, as well as research masters in in medical domain. It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers whether in data science, business analytics, market research, political science or sociology. The phenomena investigated by scientists studying humans are usually complex, thus multiple variables must be used to explain them. The theory and application of multivariate statistical models will be discussed. These models can be used to investigate the relations among many variables simultaneously, thus providing an accurate explanation of the subject of interest. The course introduces most used multivariate statistical models such as linear regression, factor analysis, analysis of (co)variance, and logistic regression. Furthermore, attention is paid to non-parametric tests. Practical application: you will learn to apply these models to data. In addition, learn how to deal with problems that occur when statistical models are used. At the end of the course, you will be able to determine which statistical model should be used to investigate different types of research questions. Furthermore, you will be able to execute the corresponding analyses and report results, conforming to APA guidelines.
topics: multivariate statistics; linear regression; factor analysis; ANOVA/ANCOVA; logistic regression; non-parametric tests
methods: Multivariate statistics; Regression analysis; Factor analysis; ANOVA/ANCOVA; Logistic regression; Non-parametric tests

name: Persuasive Communication
description2: Explores ethical persuasion and climate communication. Students learn persuasive communication models and frameworks and collaborate with climate scientists at the Delta Climate Centre to produce sustainability messaging on water, food and energy.
profile: This third-year course on ‘persuasive communication’ in the connected realms of ‘science, society and sustainability’ will build on your existing knowledge of classical rhetoric and argumentation theory and look at persuasion mostly beyond the humanities in the fields of communication studies, social psychology and neuroscience. The course has several aims. The first is to make students aware of persuasion strategies that circulate in everyday social discourses. These discourses can be found in the domains of local politics, law, advertising, business, media and governmental institutions. Students will be introduced to new theoretical frameworks and models, such as framing, nudging, cognitive shorthands and the coactive model of persuasion. Simultaneously, they will learn about the importance of the ethics of persuasive communication in given public contexts. Ethical theories that we will explore will range from utilitarianism to universalism and from dialogic ethics to situationalism. The course will build towards a significant community engaged learning (CEL) element. This is the main aim of the course; namely, to get university students out of the classroom and into the real world of work and applied skills experience. This CEL aspect will mainly take place in the second half of the semester. Here, with their newly acquired persuasive communication knowledge and skills, students will help local institutions to address and solve both internal and external communication challenges that they currently have.
topics: persuasion; framing; nudging; cognitive shortcuts; ethics of persuasion; climate communication

name: Creative Communication Laboratory
description2: Explores meaning-making through creative expression. Students study and practice poetic forms, experiment with sonic poetry, performance and other unconventional forms of communication, engage with theoretical texts and produce their own creative work.
profile: Creative Communication Laboratory is an academic course that examines how meaning is produced through imagination, experimentation, and artistic practice. Creative work is studied and developed within a framework of critical reading, analytical discussion, and reflective writing. Communication is approached as a cultural and theoretical problem shaped by language, sound, rhythm, performance, and media. You will analyze how writers and artists use language to generate meaning beyond description, and how formal deviation operates as a deliberate, historically situated practice rather than error. The first part of the course focuses on poetry and performance as foundational practices. You will progress from traditional lyric forms to bent, strained, and experimental poetry, situating these practices within literary, historical, and cultural contexts. Class emphasizes rhythm, sound, imagery, voice, and embodiment, combining close reading with creative and analytical work. In this course, poetry is treated both as a genre and as a transferable set of strategies that cultivate formal control and precision. After Spring Break and the exam, the course turns to hybrid forms and independent creative projects. You will extend poetic methods into broader creative practices, including performative, sound-based, or digitally mediated work. Final projects may not involve singing, songwriting, or music performance, and sound-based work is permitted only when sound functions as a poetic, linguistic, or conceptual material.
topics: or digitally mediated work; creative; sonic poetry; unconventional forms; poetic forms; communication

name: Introduction to Film & Media
description2: Introduces film and media as systems of meaning and cultural production. Examines how images, narratives and technologies shape perception, identity and power; covers film storytelling, representation and genres; and develops critical engagement skills.
profile: MCCMED111: Introduction to Film & Media provides you with a solid foundation in the study of film, while also introducing you briefly to media more broadly. The course begins by tracing the development of cinema from its earliest experiments to later artistic movements and innovations. This historical perspective helps you understand film not only as entertainment but also as an evolving cultural form that reflects and shapes society. At the same time, we focus on the elements of film form, such as narrative, cinematography, editing, and sound, which give you the vocabulary needed to describe and analyze how films work. Much of our attention is on film culture and analysis, since these provide the best starting point for further study in the field. Together, we examine and discuss influential examples, considering both their artistic qualities and their broader theoretical and political contexts. This approach allows you to see how films respond to social change while also experimenting with style and technique. In the final part of the course, we widen our perspective to take a short look at media more generally. By considering examples from television, streaming, and digital platforms, we make connections between film and the wider media environment and prepare the ground for more advanced courses in the cluster. Engagement with academic readings is another central part of the course. These texts present important concepts and debates that shape the study of film and media.
topics: analyze how films work; technologies shape perception; covers film storytelling; cultural production; critical engagement; media

name: Media Archaeology
description2: Explores media technologies before digital culture. Studies cassette tapes, typewriters and early printing as material objects that carry meaning; includes hands‑on experiments; no technical background required.
profile: Media Archaeology explores the cultural and material significance of pre-digital media technologies, such as cassette tapes, typewriters, and early printed books, and how they shaped the production, circulation, and preservation of knowledge. We will study these objects from multiple perspectives, combining close material analysis with broader historical and cultural interpretation. You will examine how physical properties such as weight, texture, and durability influence communication and memory. The course will include seminar discussions, critical reflections, and hands-on activities that encourage active engagement with obsolete media. Practical exercises may involve recording silence, identifying the sonic characteristics of cassette hiss, or investigating the design, use, and cultural impact of the Sony Walkman. Through these activities, we will learn to treat media as both historical evidence and lived experience, linking material form to cultural meaning. These media objects are chosen because they exemplify the theories and readings central to debates in media archaeology today. By the end of the semester, you will have developed analytical thinking, interpretive skill, and cultural awareness consistent with the aims of a liberal arts education. You will be able to explain how studying obsolete and pre-digital technologies informs our understanding of today’s media. No technical expertise is required, only curiosity and a willingness to work closely with media as physical and cultural artifacts.
topics: cassette tapes; early printed books; how they shaped the production; preservation of knowledge; durability influence communication; technical background required

name: From T.V. to TikTok
description2: Explores how media shape attitudes and provide answers through examples from TV and TikTok. Examines messages that teach fear, pity, admiration and allyship.
profile: This course examines social history and everyday life through American mainstream media from the mid-twentieth century to the present. Its central premise is threefold. First, storytelling shapes how we understand the world. Second, who gets to tell the story matters. Third, media provides insight into the past, present, and constructions for possible futures. Engaging with narratives across a wide range of media, from television and film to podcasts and TikTok, supports this point. So does amplifying the voices of the silenced and treating viral moments, such as a Justin Bieber performance clip, as cultural snapshots that reveal contemporary values, anxieties, and desires. The course opens with fear, conformity, and identity, using The Twilight Zone (1959) and Black Mirror (2011–) as bookends of the same uneasy question: what does society do to the individual? Week two then draws from future foresight methodology to explore the question: what does society imagine for itself in the future? Who is centered and who left out of the imaginations? The course then turns to mediated constructions of "reality," placing competing versions of the same story side by side and asking who the narrative serves and who it harms. Case studies include the "Hollywood Indian" versus films written, directed, and acted by Native Americans. The juxtaposition exposes how the media both marginalizes and empowers. A parallel examination of disability representation contrasts the inspirational "disabled hero" trope with authentic portrayals by differently abled people themselves.
topics: justin bieber performance clip; as cultural snapshots that reveal contemporary values; tiktok; media shape attitudes; teach fear; answers

name: Media & the Environment
description2: Examines representation of environmental concerns through visual culture. Explores the Anthropocene, animal representation, deep time, biocentrism, contested nature, indigenous and postcolonial media; analyzes how media shape environmental understanding; and includes a paper or media project.
profile: Media and the Environment examines how environmental issues are represented and debated through visual and audiovisual media. You study how media shape the ways ecological problems are understood, felt, and acted upon. The course introduces key concepts such as the Anthropocene, animal representation, deep time, biocentrism, contested ideas of nature, and indigenous and postcolonial media. You use these concepts as analytical tools to examine how environmental meaning is produced across different media forms and cultural contexts. The main goal of the course is to help you analyze environmental media critically and precisely. You learn how film, photography, sound, and digital media make ecological processes, environmental risk, and human and nonhuman relations visible and intelligible. The course emphasizes close analysis of images, narratives, and aesthetic strategies, as well as comparison across media genres and historical moments. You also examine how media translate scientific knowledge and lived experience into stories, images, and affects that shape public understanding, sustainability discourse, and political judgment. Questions of agency, scale, temporality, and responsibility guide your analysis throughout the course. The course combines sustained reading with structured discussion and applied analytical work. You work with scholarly texts, media examples, and guided exercises, and you complete either a final analytical paper or a media-based project. This combination reflects the core idea of the course.
topics: animal representation; deep time; contested ideas of nature; postcolonial media; media shape environmental; environmental concerns
